reverse_outline.summary: Promise: learn fifteen failure patterns, signs, costs and fixing chapters
Patterns are locally rational + cost hits liquidity not budgets + patterns chain from missing contract/metric/owner
Marketplace as liquidity machine; page names how it loses liquidity
Failure is slow loss of coherence, with everyday symptoms
Fifteen named patterns as shared vocabulary for the book
Uniform description format; quotes and Veldmark cases are invented
Patterns come from reasonable local decisions chaining from missing contracts, vanity metrics, unowned hand-offs
Roadmap of the page
Four families of patterns
Where along the pipeline each family strikes
Four cost dimensions used throughout
Category Straitjacket quote: new category takes weeks
Signs of hard-coded, unversioned category tree
Why: tree copied by every consumer, category acts as schema key, no owner
Costs of rigid taxonomy, with public migration example
Veldmark: Tradeyard's divergent country trees and slow category changes
Remedy: versioned, owned taxonomy with mappings and migration runbook
Chapters addressing the category straitjacket
Attribute Junkyard quote: dump into extra fields
Signs of free-form, undictionaried attributes
Why: flexible storage, local key additions, inconsistent validation, no owner
Costs of messy attributes: invisible listings, unenforceable rules, cleanup
Veldmark: thousands of sparse attribute keys at Tradeyard
Remedy: governed attribute dictionary validated on every channel
Chapters addressing attribute junkyard
Ghost Inventory quote: alert e-mail not our problem
Signs of sold or removed listings lingering in copies
Why: removal under-designed, consumers copy state on own schedules
Costs of ghost listings for liquidity, trust and money
Veldmark: Femke's sold bike in next-day alert digest; audit of stale listings
Remedy: removal as first-class event with latency objectives and send-time checks
Chapters addressing ghost inventory
Seeing Double quote: three agencies, three listings
Signs of the same item listed many times
Why: duplicates rewarded, weak keys, no owner of show-once decision
Costs of duplicates, with portal tooling example
Veldmark: Hearthly's listings-per-property ratio and multi-agency flat
Remedy: separate abusive from legitimate duplicates, cluster registry
Chapters addressing duplicates
Feed Roulette quote: wait for support to learn what happened
Signs of partner feeds ingested without contract
Why: one-off adapters, fear of rejecting paying partners, unguarded snapshots
Costs of uncontracted feeds, inventory non-exclusivity
Veldmark: truncated dealer files unpublish tens of thousands of cars
Remedy: contract per channel with envelope, error reports, mass-change guard
Chapters addressing feed roulette
Search-as-record quote: don't touch the index
Signs of search index acting as system of record
Why: teams write directly to the convenient index
Costs of an unrebuildable index
Veldmark: reindex during peak causes search outage
Remedy: index as rebuildable read model with versions and drills
Chapters addressing search as system of record
Multiplier Creep quote: just a small boost
Signs of stacked paid ranking boosts without caps
Why: monetization and ranking teams own different targets, no one owns trade-off
Costs of boosts, including EU legal exposure
Veldmark: five layers of boosts and paid share of first page
Remedy: bounded paid fields, relevance floor, caps, labels
Chapters addressing multiplier creep
Moderation-as-afterthought quote: add a queue later
Signs of trust and safety bolted on after launch
Why: T&S seen as cost center, serial checks, unversioned policies
Costs of late moderation, with leboncoin court case
Veldmark: Tradeyard moderation volumes and underestimated violation prevalence
Remedy: T&S platform in the flow with risk tiers and sampling
Chapters addressing moderation
Fast Mail for Fraudsters quote: messaging is just delivery
Signs of messaging built for speed without safety controls
Why: platform's job ends at contact, privacy avoidance, delivery metrics
Costs of inbox fraud, with UK fraud data
Veldmark: phishing link sent to Femke and rule response
Remedy: safety checks inside the message delivery path
Chapters addressing messaging fraud
Copy-Paste Country quote: separate release train per country
Signs of per-market code or reference-data copies
Why: copying was fastest entry and local autonomy has value
Costs of country copies, with Adevinta record
Veldmark: Tradeyard's four divergent country platforms and slow rule rollout
Remedy: one codebase per capability, differences as configuration
Chapters addressing copy-paste countries
Deal-Shaped Architecture quote: leave the acquired stack alone
Signs of acquired marketplaces keeping whole stacks indefinitely
Why: deal incentives, unfunded integration, regulatory limits
Costs of duplicated stacks, with acquisition synergy example
Veldmark: four of everything and cross-brand fraud and dealers
Remedy: per-capability keep/share/replatform decisions, generic first
Chapters addressing deal-shaped architecture
Forced Fit quote: central platform is mandatory
Signs of a central platform imposed where it doesn't fit
Why: synergy pressure, platform shaped by first tenant
Costs of forced platforms, with eBay reversal example
Veldmark: shared search would miss Hearthly's map needs
Remedy: platforms earned as products, mandate only narrow contracts
Chapters addressing forced fit
Vanity Liquidity quote: activity at a record
Signs of reporting activity rather than outcomes
Why: activity easy to count, outcomes need cross-system joins
Costs of vanity metrics, with public examples
Veldmark: three brands count contacts differently
Remedy: governed liquidity metrics that objectives must name
Chapters addressing vanity liquidity
Billing by Guesswork quote: which service is right on quota
Signs of entitlements checked ad hoc in many places
Why: flag-per-product growth, split ownership of catalog and billing
Costs of inconsistent entitlements
Veldmark: dealer billed overage for unpublished cars
Remedy: one entitlement service with ledger, bill from delivery
Chapters addressing billing by guesswork
Set-and-Forget AI quote: model untouched since 2021
Signs of unowned, unmonitored production models
Why: models shipped as projects, uses expand, labels go stale
Costs of ungoverned models, with Zillow Offers case
Veldmark: model inventory gaps and declined guaranteed-offer proposal
Remedy: model registry and governance by decision tier
Chapters addressing set-and-forget AI

results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All 128 aligned units' summaries match the controlling idea of their spec paragraph, in spec order (intro p001-p006, fifteen seven-unit pattern blocks p007-p114, chains p115-p120, indicators p121-p122, matrix p123-p124, conclusion p125-p128). The two callouts are apparatus, matched to no paragraph.

Introduction callout (KEY POINTS) was marked two_ideas: it is the house-style three-bullet thesis callout, which the spec places there deliberately (thesis_statement placement: 'KEY POINTS callout (all three bullets)'); it is not a paragraph with one controlling idea.

The Patterns Across the Book ¶2 was marked two_ideas ('how to read the matrix + densest columns'). Its first sentence ('Read down a column...') is the transition the spec declares for p124 (carries over 'How to read the matrix'); the controlling idea is the density finding and its consequence for group-level ownership.

Every unit aligns to a spec paragraph whose advances_thesis cites W1-W5, and its content matches that claim (signs W1, mechanism W2, cost and public record W3, chains W4, remedy/indicators/chapters W5).

results.quote: Nobody watched the control sellers, whose contacts per bump fell; why they fell was never established. After rollout to everyone, contacts per bump fell 31%.
results.finding: The bump-price episode ends on its numbers with no sentence saying what it shows (the spec's 'shows': decisions followed a number that did not measure matches, so a one-sided test approved a price that cost contacts). Both flow readers could not extract the lesson. The cause can stay unestablished while the paragraph says what the episode demonstrates.

Apart from the bump-price episode, the tables (family table, indicators table, matrix) are each followed by a paragraph saying how to read them; every figure carries a caption stating what it shows; the role quotes are glossed by the 'What it looks like' unit that follows; public examples are tied to their point ('Two public designs show the alternative', 'the public record shows mandates that reversed'); the supply-chain incident is followed by what it shows ('how fast the gap spreads').

All declared transitions hold at their boundaries: section openers (families: elaboration; chains: 'The patterns rarely appear alone' elaboration; indicators: 'Breaking a chain at its origin starts with knowing which pattern is active' problem_solution; matrix: 'The indicators table gives a number and an owner...; the matrix below gives the chapters' similarity); intro p002 contrast ('rarely fails dramatically'), p003-p006; the fixed phrase transitions of every pattern unit (quote, What it looks like, Why it happens, What it costs, An illustration, The remedy direction, Where this book helps); chain bolds p116-p119; p120 'Three patterns sit at the roots'; p122 contrast 'not targets'; p124 'Read down a column'; conclusion p126-p128. The hand-off links [[meet-veldmark]].

results.draft_locus: Fifteen Patterns to Recognize ¶32 (Feed Roulette, placed after The Attribute Junkyard, Ghost Inventory and Seeing Double); How the Patterns Reinforce Each Other ¶2
results.quote: The supply chain: Feed Roulette → The Attribute Junkyard, Ghost Inventory and Seeing Double.
results.finding: Both flow readers report that the reader meets three effects (Junkyard, Ghost Inventory, Seeing Double) before their declared cause, Feed Roulette, which comes fifth in the data family; reader B lost the thread until the chains section, reader A says the order is 'not strict pipeline order' and recommends moving Feed Roulette earlier. The order is the spec's (p038-p044 after p017-p037), and Feed Roulette is also 'on the way in', so the spec's own pipeline rationale would place it earlier.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader A, sections 1 and 4 (data-family order; 'put Feed Roulette before The Attribute Junkyard, Ghost Inventory and Seeing Double'); flow reader B item B1

results.quote: A new anti-phishing rule, written on Sunday 7 March after a fake payment link reached Femke (told under Fast Mail for Fraudsters, next), reaches Belgium only on Wednesday with the next Yardstick deploy, and never reaches Poland or Portugal.
results.finding: Both readers met the rule's consequence before its cause: the incident that motivates the rule is told only in the next section, so Femke's timeline is read Monday/Tuesday, then Sunday's rule, then Sunday's phishing. The spec's p063 evidence prescribes this forward reference ('told under Fast Mail for Fraudsters') with Moderation ordered before Fast Mail, so the fix needs a spec decision (swap the two illustrations, or move the rule's back-story into the Fast Mail illustration).
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, items B2 and B3 (reader A item A2)

results.quote: The evening alert digest, assembled at 17:30 from a database replica snapshot and never re-checked, goes out on Tuesday at 07:00 to 214 users with the bike in it.
results.finding: Both readers stopped at an 'evening' digest sent at 07:00 the next morning and had to work out which day 17:30 belongs to (Monday, before the 18:10 sale). The prose obscures a timeline the spec states clearly.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item B4 (reader A item A1)

results.quote: Nobody watched the control sellers, whose contacts per bump fell; why they fell was never established. After rollout to everyone, contacts per bump fell 31%.
results.finding: Both readers re-read the bump-price experiment and could not tell what its lesson is: the control sellers' fall is reported, the cause withheld, and nothing ties it to the one-sided test missing the cost to sellers outside it. The spec keeps the cause unestablished but states what the episode shows; the draft does not say it.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item B8 (reader A item A3)

results.quote: In October 2027 a group taxonomy service, part of the group's new shared platform, takes over the category tree.
results.finding: Both readers did not know what 'the group's new shared platform' (and, per reader B, 'the group search platform' in the Junkyard illustration) referred to: Common Ground is introduced only under Deal-Shaped Architecture and the shared search platform only under The Forced Fit, so early illustrations read as facts the reader should already know.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item B6 (reader A item A8)

results.quote: Ranking policy v1 goes live on 1 December 2027.
results.finding: Both readers had to re-read to place the figures: the sentence order is go-live, then the earlier cluster-randomized test, then results, so it is unclear whether 17% / 9.9% / -2.5% are test results or post-launch figures.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item B13 (reader A item A9)

results.quote: Femke's bike had 52 "contacts" under the old definition and 13 qualified ones, with the phisher excluded.
results.finding: Reader A (A4): 52 contacts here against '14 conversations in 24 hours' under Fast Mail sent the reader back to check; the reconciliation (old definition counts every message plus phone reveals) is left to the reader.

results.finding: Reader A (A5): the incident shows mass unpublishing and new identifiers, not junk attributes, lingering ghosts or visible duplicates, so the reader had to stop and ask how it proves the chain it illustrates.

results.finding: Reader B (B5): read literally, the domain's young age is why the link was delivered; the intended meaning is that nothing checked domain age.

results.draft_locus: How the Patterns Reinforce Each Other ¶5
results.quote: local teams route around it, and the shadow stacks recreate the archipelago.
results.finding: Reader B (B14): 'archipelago' arrives without antecedent; the prose never calls the acquired stacks an archipelago (only Figure 13's alt text does).

results.draft_locus: How the Patterns Reinforce Each Other ¶4
results.quote: A platform that checks listings only at creation, and treats copied photos as harmless duplicates, lets a fake listing reach the inbox, where the scam closes.
results.finding: Reader B (B15): the trust chain is about fake listings scamming buyers, but the only Fast Mail story is a fake buyer scamming a seller, so the chain and its worked example point in opposite directions.

results.draft_locus: How the Patterns Reinforce Each Other ¶3
results.quote: The monetization chain: Vanity Liquidity and Billing by Guesswork → Multiplier Creep.
results.finding: Reader B (section 4): Multiplier Creep is described several sections before its two roots, Vanity Liquidity and Billing by Guesswork, with no note that the roots come later.

results.quote: It does not report outcomes: qualified contacts per listing, time to first contact
results.finding: 'Qualified contact' is the measure the Vanity Liquidity remedy and illustration rest on (the 100-to-37 index, 'qualified contact v1.0', the indicators table), but the draft never says what makes a contact qualified; the only hint is 'with the phisher excluded'.

results.quote: evaluate ranking changes with two-sided guardrail metrics
results.finding: 'Two-sided guardrail metrics' is used at Multiplier Creep, in the monetization chain and in Vanity Liquidity, and is glossed only later ('guardrails for both sides of the market', Vanity Liquidity remedy); marketplace two-sidedness is on the spec's does_not_know list (marketplace economics).

results.quote: The search index has quietly become the system of record, and nobody can rebuild it from anything else.
results.finding: 'System of record as used here' is on the spec's does_not_know list; it is used in the family table before the definition given under Search as System of Record ('the one authoritative copy ... from which every other copy can be rebuilt'). The sentence itself carries most of the meaning; no flow reader reported it.

Other does_not_know terms are given at or before first use: contract and vanity metric (Introduction ¶5), category taxonomy, attributes, mandate, feed contract, read model (Ghost Inventory chapters line), monotonic versions, entitlement, T&S, DSA statements of reasons, relevance floor, cluster-randomized test, perceptual hashes, multi-homing (explained by the competition-authority quote). Both flow readers noted that 'read model' is defined only inside a 'Where this book helps' line, but it is defined there before its next use and neither reader was stopped by it, so it is not recorded as a failure. Learning to rank, percolation, DAC7 and VIN detail are not used as unexplained terms in the body.

The introduction bridges from the previous page's liquidity machine, opens the problem with concrete symptoms (sold bikes in alerts, one flat three times, a vanished dealer stock, a 2021 boost), states the thesis and gives a roadmap; it is none of placeholder, restated question, dictionary, 'dawn of man' or book report.

Using the Patterns does not open with 'in conclusion', adds no new subtopic (the legitimate-variation test is the declared synthesis), holds no body evidence, and does not end on a restated thesis alone: it ends on the callback and the hand-off to [[meet-veldmark]].

Using the Patterns ¶3 states what no single section states ('That test is what the fifteen patterns share: each is a variation that nobody decided, owned or measured, and its remedy is the same in kind'), and ¶2 and ¶4 say why it matters: look upstream before funding a downstream remedy, because the cheapest fix is a contract, an owner or a metric definition.

Using the Patterns ¶4 returns to the opening symptoms and names each: the sold bike in Tuesday's alert e-mails is Ghost Inventory, the flat three times is Seeing Double, the vanished dealer stock is Feed Roulette, the 2021 boost is Multiplier Creep, each traced to a missing contract, owner or metric.

The cold reader of the opening predicted the fifteen patterns in four families with the full per-pattern template (quote, signs, mechanism, cost, Veldmark illustration, remedy, chapters), then the chains, the first indicators, the chapter map and how to use the names; evidence as composite role quotes, documented public examples and an invented Veldmark; a declarative, blame-free tone. This matches the roadmap and AC-3's expected answer.

The reader named Feed Roulette (a truncated snapshot under 'absence means delete' unpublishing the omitted cars, which search and alerts then faithfully copy) and placed the first fix at the feed/ingestion contract ('break the chain at the contract, not at the index': mass-change guard, stable keys, validation, error reports) rather than search or alerts, and named the follow-on patterns. Matches the expected answer (Feed Roulette leading to a removal problem; fix the feed contract first).

The reader named Multiplier Creep, its upstream roots Vanity Liquidity and Billing by Guesswork (the monetization chain), and the chapters ranking, monetization-models, products-and-entitlements, advertising-platforms, experimentation and marketplace-regulation (plus liquidity, data platform and a case). Matches the expected answer.
